oil.summary: Crude pulled back Thursday — WTI off 1.19% to $101.21/bbl, Brent off 1.64% to $104.09 — on de-escalation signals after Reuters reported China is pressing Iran to rein in Houthi activity, and separately, US-Houthi talks were confirmed to be opening. The selloff in crude products was far sharper: RBOB crashed 8.16% and Heating Oil shed 8.04%, likely a demand-side relief trade on the inventory beat reported in US gasoline stocks. Despite today's dip, both benchmarks are up roughly 14-19% on the month, reflecting six-plus months of Middle East supply disruption. The legislative backdrop remains hawkish: the US House passed the Graham bill authorizing 100% tariffs on countries — notably India and China — purchasing Russian crude. Ukraine's strike on a Rosneft/Gazprom Neft co-owned refinery near Moscow adds further upside risk to product markets, while Kpler's Matt Smith maintained a constructive medium-term view on crude as the diesel crunch deepens.
drivers: De-escalation signals — China pressing Iran on Houthis and US-Houthi talks opening — triggered a crude pullback despite an otherwise tight physical market
RBOB and Heating Oil plunged ~8% each, potentially linked to a reported US gasoline inventory build and demand-side relief pricing
US House passage of Graham Russia sanctions bill, threatening 100% tariffs on Indian and Chinese buyers of Russian crude, raises long-term supply-route risk

gas.summary: Henry Hub eased 0.93% to $2.864/MMBtu while TTF slipped 1.30% to €77.015/MWh on the day, though the monthly picture tells a very different story — TTF is up 21% over the past 30 days as the Middle East crisis sustains LNG premium pricing globally. The macro narrative remains bullish: UK energy bills are forecast to jump 25-30% in Q1 2027 as the crisis drags on. Russia's swift cutoff of gas to Armenia — days after Yerevan announced plans to diversify away from Moscow — underscores the continued weaponization of gas flows. Separately, Taiwan is actively reconsidering nuclear power to reduce LNG exposure, a signal of how structurally stressed the global gas market has become. A reported temporary closure of a key Saudi Hormuz-bypass pipeline adds further upside tail risk to LNG spot pricing.
drivers: TTF up 21% on the month as prolonged Middle East crisis squeezes LNG supply routes; today's dip appears technical after a sharp run-up
Russia cut gas to Armenia immediately after diversification announcement, highlighting the continued use of gas as geopolitical leverage
Taiwan moving toward nuclear revival and UK facing 25-30% energy bill increases in early 2027 — both signal that high gas prices are forcing structural demand responses

power.summary: EU Carbon EUAs nudged up 1.35% to $81.62/EUA, continuing a modest uptrend that has the contract up 4.64% over the past month. The carbon move is modest relative to the broader energy complex but directionally consistent with elevated gas prices keeping coal-to-gas switching economics in flux. The key structural headlines today: Taiwan is reassessing nuclear as soaring LNG costs make its current power mix untenable, and Turkey announced a $108 billion, ten-year renewable buildout targeting 120 GW of wind and solar — though Ankara is simultaneously expanding oil and gas. Carbon-market specific news flow is thin today; the EUA move looks technically driven and anchored to the broader energy-price environment rather than any single catalyst.
drivers: EUAs +1.35% on the day, supported by elevated TTF gas prices keeping carbon abatement incentives firm despite today's slight TTF pullback
Taiwan's nuclear revival signals structurally high LNG costs are forcing power-sector pivots, with broader implications for global gas and carbon demand
Turkey's $108 billion renewables commitment (120 GW wind/solar target) is a notable long-term carbon-demand headwind, though near-term power-market impact is limited
